questions.prompt: What real-world gap does this course's opening lesson identify?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: The gap between a model that works as Python code and a stable, network-reachable API another program can call

Turning working model code into something callable over a network with a stable contract is exactly the product-engineering gap this course addresses.
keyPoints: Turning working model code into something callable over a network with a stable contract is exactly the product-engineering gap this course addresses.

questions.prompt: What does Pydantic validation prevent from happening, for a malformed request?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: It rejects the request with a clear error before any application code, including an LLM call, executes

Validation acts as a gate that catches problems before they propagate into expensive or incorrect downstream processing.
keyPoints: Validation acts as a gate that catches problems before they propagate into expensive or incorrect downstream processing.

questions.prompt: Why does the cost of an extra request matter more for rate limiting an LLM-calling endpoint than a typical CRUD endpoint?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Because each LLM API call has a real dollar cost, so an unrate-limited endpoint risks running up a large bill quickly from a bug or an attacker

The direct financial cost per LLM call raises the stakes of unrestricted request volume well above what a typical free CRUD operation would risk.
keyPoints: The direct financial cost per LLM call raises the stakes of unrestricted request volume well above what a typical free CRUD operation would risk.

questions.prompt: Why does streaming improve a user's experience of an LLM response, even without changing total generation time?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Because the user sees tokens appearing immediately instead of experiencing a blank wait for the full response, improving perceived latency

Streaming addresses perceived latency — the user's experience of waiting — separately from the actual total time the underlying generation takes.
keyPoints: Streaming addresses perceived latency — the user's experience of waiting — separately from the actual total time the underlying generation takes.

questions.prompt: Why is holding an HTTP connection open for a multi-hour fine-tuning job impractical?
questions.referenceAnswer: Real-world network conditions and worker availability make holding a connection open for hours fundamentally unreliable, motivating an asynchronous approach instead.
keyPoints: Real-world network conditions and worker availability make holding a connection open for hours fundamentally unreliable, motivating an asynchronous approach instead.

choices.text: Because the connection can drop, time out, or block a worker for an impractically long time
Because HTTP connections cannot exceed one second by protocol design
Because fine-tuning jobs never take more than a few seconds
Because APIs cannot accept requests related to fine-tuning at all

questions.prompt: What is a key drawback of polling for job status compared to webhooks?
questions.referenceAnswer: Repeated, often-unnecessary status checks and delayed notification are the direct costs of a polling approach compared to an immediate callback.
keyPoints: Repeated, often-unnecessary status checks and delayed notification are the direct costs of a polling approach compared to an immediate callback.

choices.text: It wastes requests checking a job that hasn't changed status, and introduces delay bounded by the polling interval
Polling requires the client to expose a publicly reachable endpoint
Polling always executes the job twice
Polling is impossible to implement in any programming language

questions.prompt: What is the N+1 query problem?
questions.referenceAnswer: The N+1 pattern is a common inefficiency where a loop of individual queries replaces what could have been one or two well-designed queries.
keyPoints: The N+1 pattern is a common inefficiency where a loop of individual queries replaces what could have been one or two well-designed queries.

choices.text: Fetching a list of items, then running a separate query for each item's related data in a loop, turning one query into many
Running exactly one query per application, with no exceptions
A database configuration error that prevents any queries from running
A caching strategy for reducing database load

questions.prompt: Why is hardcoding an API key directly in source code a serious risk?
questions.referenceAnswer: Version control history retains old commits indefinitely, so a hardcoded secret remains exposed to anyone with repo access even after being 'removed' in a later commit.
keyPoints: Version control history retains old commits indefinitely, so a hardcoded secret remains exposed to anyone with repo access even after being 'removed' in a later commit.

choices.text: It ends up permanently in version control history, visible to anyone with repository access, even after later removal
It makes the application run measurably faster
It is the only way to authenticate an API call
It has no security implications as long as the repository is private

questions.prompt: Streaming responses are interrupted and users retry requests. What would you inspect first, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Trace client disconnects, server timeouts and proxy buffering. Make side effects idempotent across retries. Test cancellation and partial-output handling.
keyPoints: Trace client disconnects, server timeouts and proxy buffering.
Make side effects idempotent across retries.
Test cancellation and partial-output handling.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Test cancellation and partial-output handling. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Test cancellation and partial-output handling.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Trace client disconnects, server timeouts and proxy buffering. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Trace client disconnects, server timeouts and proxy buffering.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.
